pages.title: The Blanket of Air: Earth's Atmosphere
bulletPoints: Earth is wrapped in a protective cocoon of air called the atmosphere that gives us the weather we experience.
The troposphere: The lowest layer of air where clouds float, raindrops form, and gentle winds blow.
The Sun is the giant engine powering all weather by heating our land, oceans, and air unevenly.
Observation: Look at the sky right now—are the clouds moving fast or drifting lazily in the breeze?

pages.title: Temperature: Hot, Warm, Cool, and Cold
bulletPoints: Thermometers measure temperature in degrees Celsius (°C) and Fahrenheit (°F).
When the sun is high at noon, sunlight shines straight down and heats the ground quickly.
When the sun is low in early morning or evening, its rays are spread out, feeling cool and pleasant.
Warm air is lighter and floats upward, while cool air is dense and sinks gently toward the ground.

pages.title: Winds & Breezes: Air on the Move
bulletPoints: Wind is simply air moving from high pressure cool areas toward warm, low pressure areas.
Sea breeze: During the sunny day, cool air blows off the ocean onto warm beach sand.
Land breeze: At night, the ocean stays warmer than land, so air blows gently back out to sea.
Anemometers spin around to measure wind speed, while wind vanes point out wind directions (North, South, East, West).

pages.title: The Magical Water Cycle: Evaporation
bulletPoints: Evaporation: Warm yellow sunshine heats puddles, lakes, and oceans, turning liquid water into invisible water vapor.
Transpiration: Green trees and plant leaves release tiny water droplets into the air through microscopic stomata.
Invisible rise: Warm, moist air rises high up into the cooler upper sky.
Experiment: Put a shallow dish of water in the sun and watch it slowly evaporate over the afternoon!

pages.title: Condensation & Cloud Formation
bulletPoints: Condensation: As warm water vapor rises into the cold sky, it cools down and turns back into tiny water droplets.
Cloud condensation nuclei: Water droplets cling to microscopic bits of airborne sea salt and dust.
Billions of these floating droplets gather together to form fluffy white clouds in the blue sky.
Fog: A cloud that forms right down on the ground on cold autumn mornings!

pages.title: Meet the Clouds: Cirrus, Cumulus, and Stratus
bulletPoints: Cirrus clouds: High, feathery wisps of ice crystals looking like horse tails high in the blue sky.
Cumulus clouds: Big, bright white, fluffy cotton-ball clouds that signal sunny pleasant weather.
Stratus clouds: Low, flat, grey blankets covering the entire sky like a giant bedsheet, bringing light drizzle.
Cumulonimbus: Towering dark thunderstorm anvils reaching miles into the sky with lightning inside!

pages.title: Precipitation: Raindrops Falling Down
bulletPoints: When cloud droplets collide and grow too heavy to float in the air, gravity pulls them down as rain.
Rain gauges catch rainwater in clear measuring cylinders to track how many millimeters of rain fell.
The smell of fresh rain: Petrichor is the delightful earthy perfume released when raindrops hit dry soil.
Rain fills bubbling mountain streams, waters farmers' green crops, and fills our drinking water reservoirs.

pages.title: Thunder & Lightning: Nature's Fireworks
bulletPoints: Static electricity: Ice crystals and water droplets bounce inside storm clouds, building up electric charges.
Lightning: A super-hot giant electric spark leaping between clouds or striking down toward the ground.
Lightning is hotter than the surface of the sun: It instantly heats the surrounding air, making it expand explosively.
Thunder: That explosive expansion of air creates the rolling, booming acoustic sound wave we call thunder!

pages.title: Rainbows: Sunlight & Prisms in the Sky
bulletPoints: White sunlight looks clear, but it is actually a blend of seven vibrant colors (VIBGYOR).
Refraction: When sunlight enters a curved round raindrop, the water bends and separates the light rays.
Internal reflection: The light bounces off the back of the raindrop and shines back toward our eyes.
The magic rainbow arc: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, and Red painted across the sky!

pages.title: Snowflakes: Winter's Hexagonal Crystals
bulletPoints: When cloud temperatures drop below freezing (0°C / 32°F), water vapor freezes directly into ice crystals.
Hexagonal geometry: Every water molecule forms six-sided symmetric crystal arms as it grows.
No two snowflakes are alike: Each crystal experiences a unique journey through cloud moisture and wind.
Snow blanket: A thick layer of fluffy white snow acts like insulation, keeping hibernating animals warm underneath.

pages.title: Hail & Sleet: Frozen Sky Pellets
bulletPoints: Sleet: Raindrops that freeze into small clear ice pellets as they fall through a layer of freezing air near the ground.
Hailstones: Thunderstorm updrafts toss water droplets high into freezing cloud tops over and over again.
Layer upon layer of ice freezes around the hailstone like an onion until it becomes too heavy and falls.
Hailstones can range from the size of small garden peas to large icy golf balls!

pages.title: The Dance of the Earth: Why We Have Seasons
bulletPoints: Earth revolves around the sun once every 365 days while spinning on its tilted axis (23.5 degrees).
Tilted toward the Sun: When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the sun, it enjoys long sunny days of Summer.
Tilted away from the Sun: The hemisphere tilted away receives indirect sunlight and experiences Winter.
The Equator: Regions near the middle of Earth receive direct sunshine all year round, staying warm and tropical.

pages.title: Spring: Awakening & Blossoms
bulletPoints: Spring brings longer days, warmer afternoon sunshine, and refreshing gentle rains.
Dormant brown seeds wake up in the soil and push tiny green shoots toward the light.
Fruit orchards burst into sweet pink and white blossoms as honeybees buzz happily from petal to petal.
Baby animals: Woolly lambs frolic in green meadows, ducklings hatch, and birds sing joyous morning songs.

pages.title: Summer: Sunshine & Long Golden Days
bulletPoints: Summer features the longest days and shortest nights of the entire year.
Summer Solstice: The longest day of the year (around June 21 in the Northern Hemisphere).
Sun protection: Wearing wide-brimmed sun hats, drinking cool water, and resting under shady leafy banyan trees.
Sweet summer treats: Juicy watermelons, ripe golden mangoes, ice pops, and splashing in cool swimming pools.

pages.title: The Monsoon: The Great Rain Festival
bulletPoints: Monsoon winds: Giant seasonal winds blow off the warm Indian Ocean carrying heavy moisture-laden clouds.
The parched brown earth drinks up rainwater and turns into a lush, emerald green paradise in days.
Farmers rejoice as rainwater fills irrigation canals for rice paddies and sugar cane fields.
Splashing in puddles: Floating colorful paper boats down bubbling curbside streams under big umbrellas.

pages.title: Autumn: Crisp Breezes & Falling Leaves
bulletPoints: Autumn Equinox: Day and night are of equal twelve-hour length as sunlight gently softens.
Deciduous trees stop making chlorophyll and reveal brilliant golden-yellow, amber, and crimson leaves.
Harvest festival: Farmers harvest golden wheat, pumpkins, sweet corn, and crisp juicy apples.
Animals prepare for winter: Squirrels collect and bury acorns; geese fly south in elegant V-formations.

pages.title: Winter: Frost, Blankets & Cozy Fireplaces
bulletPoints: Winter brings the shortest days, longest starry nights, and frosty morning grass.
Winter Solstice: The shortest day of the year (around December 21 in the Northern Hemisphere).
Cozy comfort: Warm woolen sweaters, fluffy mittens, steaming mugs of hot cocoa, and fuzzy socks.
Winter sleep: Groundhogs, bears, and chipmunks curl up in underground burrows to hibernate until spring.

pages.title: Extreme Weather: Hurricanes & Tornadoes
bulletPoints: Hurricanes: Giant spinning ocean storms fueled by warm tropical seawater with winds over 120 km/h.
The Eye of the Storm: The very center of a hurricane is surprisingly calm, sunny, and peaceful.
Tornadoes: Fast spinning funnels of wind that drop down from violent supercell thunderstorm clouds.
Early warning systems: Weather radar satellites and meteorologists track storms to keep families safe.

pages.title: How Meteorologists Predict the Weather
bulletPoints: Weather satellites orbit hundreds of kilometers above Earth taking continuous photographs of spinning cloud banks.
Weather balloons carry sensor boxes (radiosondes) high into the sky to measure temperature, humidity, and wind.
Supercomputers run complex physical fluid dynamics equations to simulate tomorrow's weather forecast.
Five-day forecast: Helping farmers plan harvests, pilots fly safe flight routes, and families pack umbrellas.

pages.title: Climate Care: Loving Our Weather & Earth
bulletPoints: Weather is what happens today; climate is the long-term pattern of weather over thirty years or more.
Greenhouse effect: Carbon dioxide and greenhouse gases act like a blanket trapping solar warmth.
Caring for our climate: Planting trees, riding bicycles, turning off unused lights, and recycling paper.
Earth celebration: Every season brings its own special wonder, from fresh spring blooms to quiet winter snow!
